nameStory: The bronzed cutworm moth gets its name from the metallic bronze sheen that glimmers across its wings, especially visible when light hits them at the right angle. The 'cutworm' part refers to its caterpillar stage, which has the unfortunate habit of chewing through plant stems right at ground level, effectively 'cutting' down young plants.
description: The bronzed cutworm moth is a medium-sized night-flying moth with a wingspan of about 1.6 inches across. Its wings display subtle bronze and brown tones that help it blend perfectly with tree bark during the day. Like most moths in the cutworm family, it has a sturdy, fuzzy body and holds its wings horizontally when at rest. You're most likely to spot these moths attracted to porch lights or other outdoor lighting during summer and fall evenings.

idTips.label: Wing coloration
idTips.description: Wings show a distinctive bronze or coppery sheen over brown base colors, most noticeable when light hits them directly

idTips.label: Wing size
idTips.description: Medium-sized with wings spanning about 40mm (roughly 1.6 inches) from tip to tip

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Fuzzy, robust body typical of cutworm moths, feels soft and dense if handled gently

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Subtle darker markings create shadowy patterns across the bronze background, giving it the alternate name 'shaded umber moth'

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: Holds wings horizontally when at rest, pressed flat against surfaces like tree bark or building walls

habitat: Bronzed cutworm moths can be found throughout New England in areas where grasses grow, from suburban lawns and agricultural fields to meadows and forest edges. They're particularly common around farms and gardens since their caterpillars feed on various grasses and crops. Look for the adult moths near outdoor lights in both rural and suburban settings.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active yet. Caterpillars may be found feeding on grass roots and stems in warmer late spring weather.
seasonality.summer: Adult moths begin emerging in July and are active on warm nights, often attracted to outdoor lighting. Peak flight activity occurs during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Moths continue flying through September and into October, with numbers gradually declining as temperatures drop. Late fall may still produce occasional sightings on warm nights.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active. The species overwinters in earlier life stages, waiting for spring warmth to continue their development cycle.

funFact: The caterpillars of bronzed cutworm moths are underground ninjas that can completely sever a corn stalk or garden plant at soil level in a single night, leading frustrated gardeners to find their healthy plants mysteriously toppled over by morning with no visible culprit in sight.
confusionNotes: Bronzed cutworm moths can be confused with other brown nocturnal moths, but the metallic bronze sheen on their wings is distinctive. Memory trick: Think 'bronze coins' when you see that coppery glint in your porch light - that's your cutworm moth.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cutworm' moths, the adults themselves don't cut anything - they're actually important nighttime pollinators. It's only their caterpillar stage that earns the family its notorious reputation among gardeners and farmers.
compareHints: The bronzed cutworm moth is the only species in its genus Nephelodes found in New England, making it unique in this regard. Compared to other cutworm moths in the Noctuidae family, it stands out with its distinctive bronze metallic sheen, while most relatives display duller brown or gray coloration without the coppery highlights.
